Background and significance. Fatty liver disease affects roughly a quarter of adults worldwide, and a minority of patients progress to fibrosis and cirrhosis. Large population studies have linked progression to metabolic syndrome, diet and alcohol intake, but they cannot resolve the order of events at the tissue level. Our group has spent five years building organoid and mouse models that capture early stellate cell activation. In the ongoing Pallisade pilot, the bile acid analogue lowered serum ALT by 18% at week 8 relative to baseline, although the confidence interval is still wide and the effect needs confirmation. These observations motivate the present proposal, which asks whether early bile acid remodelling is a cause or a consequence of fibrogenesis. We will combine longitudinal sampling, spatial transcriptomics and targeted metabolomics, and we will test causal hypotheses in germ-free mice colonised with defined communities. The expected outcome is a mechanistic model that can guide the choice of endpoints for a larger trial.

text:
Please proofread this section of my fellowship application and flag anything that sounds overclaimed.

Significance. Fatty liver disease is now the most common chronic liver condition in high-income countries. Landmark cohorts such as the Rotterdam Study and UK Biobank have shown that fibrosis stage, not steatosis alone, predicts liver-related mortality, and a meta-analysis by Taylor and colleagues reported a hazard ratio of 2.9 for stage F2 versus F0. Randomised trials have tested several drug classes; one widely cited phase 3 trial reported fibrosis improvement in 24% of treated patients versus 12% on placebo. Despite this progress, we still lack biomarkers that predict who will progress. My project will address this gap by combining longitudinal stool metagenomics with targeted bile acid profiling. Following standard practice, I will treat p < 0.05 after false discovery rate correction as significant, and I have budgeted for 120 participants per group, which gives 80% power to detect a moderate effect (d = 0.4). The host department, Westmoor University's Centre for Liver Research, provides the necessary sequencing and animal facilities, and the work will be carried out in the Lindqvist lab.
note: Long negative: public cohorts, published numbers, power calculation and our own lab only.
